# Introduction

The following code relates to the **Imputation** section of the
**Editing and Imputation** learning resource on the [Analysis for Action]([PLACEHOLDER])
platform.

This course does not cover the theory of any of the methods specified. The theory of these methods are covered in the Introduction to Editing and Imputation learning resource. Additionally, this course provides an introduction to using editing and imputation methods in R. It does not teach the best method to use and when, as this is very dependent upon the dataset you are using. Instead, it only shows how different methods can be used in R.

## Troubleshooting

If you encounter any issues running the code snippets, consider the following
troubleshooting steps:
- Ensure you have followed the setup instructions in the
[README.md](../../../README.md) file including `install.packages()` for
required packages.
- Run code from top to bottom to ensure all dependencies are met.
- Restart your R session and clear all outputs.
- For more detailed troubleshooting guidance, refer to the
[troubleshooting document]([PLACEHOLDER]).

# Packages and data

Before running the code snippets, ensure you have:
- followed the setup instructions in the [README.md](README.md) file,
- install the required packages
- run the code block below.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
# Load in the following packages

library(tidyverse)
library(VIM)
library(mice)
library(here)

# Load in data
# Use here::here() to construct paths, do not setwd()
here::here()
clean_survey_data <- read_csv(here::here("Data","cleaned_data.csv"))

```

# Model-based imputation

Model-based imputation is the approximation of missing values using assumptions about the distribution of the data, 
which includes mean and median imputation. Or using assumptions about the relationship between variables or units, 
which includes ratio and regression imputation.

This code will cover one of the most common model-based imputation methods  - mean imputation. 

## Mean imputation

In this section, the `mice` package will be use to impute the missing values in the `clean_survey_data`. 
Mice stand for Multivariate Imputation via Chained Equations and it is one of the commonly used packages by R users. 
While the MICE package is able to perform multiple imputation, here we only want to use single imputation, therefore m will be set to 1.

MICE assumes that the missing data are Missing at Random (MAR), which means that the probability that a value is missing depends only on the observed value and can be predicted using them. 
It imputes data on a variable by variable basis by specifying an imputation model per variable.

```{r}
# Create a flag before imputation
age_imputed <- ifelse(is.na(clean_survey_data$age), TRUE, FALSE)

# Perform mean imputation using MICE
# method used is "mean" and m = 1 means single imputation
# maxit is a scalar giving the number of iterations (default is 5)
mean_impute <- mice(clean_survey_data, method = 'mean', m = 1, maxit = 1)
```

The mice package imputes the missing values in all variables. However in this case, “mean” imputation can only be used for numerical data, therefore the package has only imputed numerical variables, in this case 'age' and 'hours_worked_away_7d'.

You can use other imputation methods by running the methods(mice) command which gives a list of the available imputation methods. 

Next, look at the missing value and their corresponding imputed values:

```{r}
# Selecting the rows in the age column which have imputed values
mean_impute$imp$age
```

As you can see 18 missing values in the age column have been imputed, with the mean being 49.3 (1dp).

Now using the complete() function, the missing values will be replaced with the imputed values in the data set.

```{r}
# Store imputed data using complete() function
mean_data <- mice::complete(mean_impute) 

# Add the imputation flags
mean_data$age_imputed <- age_imputed
```

Now, compare the summary statistics of the age column in both data sets.

```{r}
# Summary statistics of age for original data

summary(clean_survey_data$age)
```

```{r}
# Summary statistics of age for imputed data

summary(mean_data$age)
```
Comparing the original and imputed data shows that the median age is lower in the imputed data than the original data, but all other values have stayed the same.


### Exercise

1. Using mice() function, impute the missing values in the clean_survey_data data.

2. Store the imputed data using the complete() function.

3. Look at the difference in the standard deviation of the hours_worked_away_7d column in imputed data and original data.

Impute the missing values for `hours_worked_away_7d` using mean imputation. 

```{r}

# Create a flag before imputation
hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- ifelse(is.na(clean_survey_data$hours_worked_away_7d), TRUE, FALSE)

# Perform mean imputation using MICE
mean_impute <- mice(clean_survey_data, method = 'mean', m = 1, maxit = 1)

# Store imputed data using complete() function
mean__data <- mice::complete(mean_impute) 

# Add the imputation flags
mean__data$hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- hours_worked_away_7d_flag


# Standard deviation of hours_worked_away_7d for original data 

sd(clean_survey_data$hours_worked_away_7d, na.rm = TRUE)

# Standard deviation of hours_worked_away_7d for imputed data 

sd(mean_data$hours_worked_away_7d, na.rm = TRUE)
```
The value for the imputed data, 17.08 (2dp) is lower than the original data, 17.53 (2dp). This is expected since mean imputation reduces the variance of the imputed variables because the imputation method adds more observations which are the mean - and so this reduces the average deviation from the mean for the data.
	

## Regression imputation

This section will focus on applying a regression imputation to the data. As covered before there are two types of regression imputation.

Deterministic: this method assumes that the imputed values appear close to the regression line.

Stochastic: it is an improvement to the previous method by aiming to preserve the variability of data by adding an error (residual) factor to the predicted value.

In this section, regression imputation will be performed on the hours_worked_away_7d. As all the missing record are for employed individuals, the code will first filter by employment status. The aim for this regression is to impute for genuine item non-response among people that the question applies to, rather than trying to impute working hours for someone who does not work.

## Determinstic imputation

Before carrying out imputation, check that variables have been assigned an appropriate data type. For example, categorical variables that you want to used in the model, such as sex and region, should be stored as factors in R. While numerical variables such as age and number of days should be stored as numeric or integer variables. The variable type can affect how an imputation method treats the data.

```{r}
# Select employed respondents only
employed_data <- clean_survey_data |>
  dplyr::filter(employment_status == "Employed")

# Change categorical variables to factors
employed_data$sex <- as.factor(employed_data$sex)
employed_data$region <- as.factor(employed_data$region)

# Create a flag before imputation
hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- ifelse(is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d), TRUE, FALSE)

# Deterministic regression imputation
# method used is "norm.predict"
# m = 1 means single imputation

deter_reg_impute <- mice::mice(employed_data, method = "norm.predict", m = 1) 
```

The variables that have been imputed are age and hours_worked_away_7d


```{r}
# Store data
deter_reg_data <- mice::complete(deter_reg_impute)

# Add the imputation flags
deter_reg_data$hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- hours_worked_away_7d_flag
```

### Note on predictor variables
As the code has not specifically stated any predictor variables, mice creates a predictor matrix and uses the variables available to predict the target variable(s), excluding the variable from predicting itself. The predictor matrix controls this: 1 means a variable is used as a predictor and 0 means it is not.

```{r}

# See what variables are being used as predictors
deter_reg_impute$predictorMatrix
```
For example, here you can see that mice is using age, sex, region and days_unable_28d to impute hours_worked_away_7d. 
You can explicitly modify this matrix to specify which variables should be used as predictors.

```{r}
pred <- mice::make.predictorMatrix(employed_data)

# Don't use any predictors initially
pred[,] <- 0

# Use age and sex to predict hours worked
pred[
  "hours_worked_away_7d",
  c("age", "sex")
] <- 1


deter_reg_impute_age_sex <- mice::mice(employed_data, method = "norm.predict", predictorMatrix = pred, m = 1)

# Check what variables are being used as predictors
deter_reg_impute_age_sex$predictorMatrix
```

However, mice may remove some predictors if they are not suitable for the imputation model, for example if they contain no variation or are highly related to another predictor. You can check the predictor matrix after running mice to see which predictors were used.

## Stochastic imputation
Similar code can be used for stochastic regression imputation. You only have to change the method from method = "norm.predict" to method = "norm.nob" as shown below:

```{r}

# Stochastic regression imputation
# method used is "norm.nob"
# m = 1 means single imputation

sto_reg_impute <- mice::mice(employed_data, method = "norm.nob", m = 1)
```

```{r}
# Store data

sto_reg_data <- mice::complete(sto_reg_impute) 
```


Now, you can compare graphically check how well the missing data imputations worked:

```{r}
# Graphical comparison of deterministic and stochastic regression imputation
# Both plots in one graphic

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) 

# Deterministic regression imputation plot
# Plot of observed values

plot(employed_data$age[!is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
     deter_reg_data$hours_worked_away_7d[!is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
     main = "Deterministic Regression",
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Hours worked away from home last week")

# Plot of imputed values         

points(employed_data$age[is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
         deter_reg_data$hours_worked_away_7d[is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
        col = "red")

# Regression slope

abline(lm(hours_worked_away_7d ~ age, deter_reg_data), col = "#1b98e0", lwd = 1.5) 


# Stochastic regression imputation
# Plot of observed values

plot(employed_data$age[!is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)], 
     sto_reg_data$hours_worked_away_7d[!is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
     main = "Stochastic Regression",
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Hours worked away from home last week")

# Plot of imputed values

points(employed_data$age[is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],
       sto_reg_data$hours_worked_away_7d[is.na(employed_data$hours_worked_away_7d)],     
       col = "red")

# Regression slope

abline(lm(hours_worked_away_7d ~ age, sto_reg_data), col = "#1b98e0", lwd = 1.5) 
```
In these graphs, the black points are observed values, whereas the imputed values are represented by red points. The graph visualises the main drawback of deterministic regression imputation, which is that the imputed values (red bubbles) are very close to the regression slope (blue line).

In contrast, for stochastic regression, the distribution of imputed values is similar compared to the observed values and much more realistic. The idea of adding randomly selected residuals in this approach is what forms the basis of more advanced imputation techniques. However as covered in the main Editing and Imputation learning resource, there are some disadvantages of using stochastic regression. For example, stochastic imputation can sometimes generate values outside the valid range of the variable. Imputed values should therefore be checked against appropriate validation rules.

Remember: as covered in the Introduction to editing and imputation course, stochastic regression may impute different values each time.


# Donor-based imputation

This section will focus on using donor-based imputation, where missing values for a one unit (the recipient) are replaced with observed values from another unit (the donor). The builds upon the theory for each type of donor-based imputation that is covered in the Introduction to Editing and Imputation.

## Random hot deck

In random hot deck imputation, imputation classes (also known as donor pools or adjustment cells) are formed based on matching variables. For each recipient unit `i` in a given imputation class, the potential donors are units within that same class but with the target variable `y` observed. Of these potential donors, one is selected at random typically through equal-probability sampling and used to impute the recipient. To conduct the hot deck imputation, the code below will use a small part of the `clean_survey_data`, using only 10 rows in order to make the section easier to understand. Later, the full data set will be used when covering hierarchical hot deck imputation.

```{r}
# Create a shorter data with 10 rows and all columns

shorter_data <- clean_survey_data[1:10,]

# Display the results

shorter_data

```


Here, this example will make the imputation classes by age groups. This is only an example due to the small dataset size, however real world imputation classes can use multiple domain variables to create imputation classes, for example age group AND sex AND general health. 

The code will impute the missing value in the vaccination_status variable for person number 7 (the recipient) using the matching variable age_group.

```{r}

# Define age_group variable
shorter_data <- shorter_data |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
      age >= 18 & age <= 34 ~ "18-34",
      age >= 35 & age <= 49 ~ "35-49",
      age >= 50 & age <= 64 ~ "50-64",
      age >= 65 & age <= 79 ~ "65-79",
      age >= 80             ~ "80+",
      TRUE                  ~ NA_character_
    )
  )


# Using hotdeck function in VIM package to carry out random hot deck imputation
# variable equal to the variable you want to impute
# domain_var is the variable for building domains and impute within these domains

VIM::hotdeck(data = shorter_data, variable = "vaccination_status", domain_var = "age_group" )

```

So the value for vaccination can be  “1 dose” or "2 doses” since the donors are the second, fifth and eight person (because they are in the age group 50-64). Since this is a random hot deck imputation that means the donor is randomly selected so the imputed value can be either value.

Also, there is a new column vaccination_status_imp which returns a boolean value TRUE if the missing value in the vaccination_status variable has been imputed and FALSE otherwise.


### Exercise

Carry out random hot deck imputation to impute the missing value in the general_health variable for the fifth person in the shorter data using the matching variable sex. Remember shorter data contains the first 10 observations from the clean_survey_data set.

```{r}

# Using hotdeck function in VIM package to carry out random hot deck imputation on general_health
# Sex as domain variable
VIM::hotdeck(data = shorter_data, variable = "general_health", domain_var = "sex" )
```

Here the potential imputed values could be 'Fair, 'Good' or 'Very Good'. 



## Sequential hot deck

In sequential hot deck imputation, the data set is not explicitly split into groups. Instead, the records are a set in order and each missing value is imputed by the last observed value from a record with the same matching variables.

In other words, the recipient is imputed using a donor that has the last unit y observed, belongs to the same imputation class and comes before the recipient in the data file.  In this sequential hot deck example, age group will be used again as the matching variable. However, here ord_var will also be used to specify which variable(s) the data will be sorted by, ahead of sequential hot-deck imputation.


```{r}
# Using hotdeck function in VIM package to carry out sequential hot deck imputation
# variable is the column that you want to impute
# domain_var is the matching variable
# ord_var is the variable for sorting the data set before imputation

print(VIM::hotdeck(data = shorter_data, variable = "vaccination_status", domain_var =  "age_group", 
             ord_var = "general_health"))

```
This time, the imputed value for the `vaccination_status` variable is "1 dose" because when the data is ordered by `general_health` variable, the structure of the data looks like this:

```{r}
# Arranging the general_health column in the ascending order

shorter_data |>
  dplyr::arrange(general_health)
```

As you can see, when the data is ordered by the `general_health` variable, the structure of the data changes where the recipient is the eight person and the donor is the seventh person, who is within the same age_group.

Remember shorter data contains the first 10 observations from the clean_survey_data data set.


Therefore, the donor is P0002 and the imputed value is "Good".


## K Nearest Neighbours (KNN)

Nearest neighbour donor imputation removes the restriction that the donor and the recipient have identical values for all matching variables. Instead, the matching variables are used to define a distance function between the recipient and a potential donor.

An extension of this concept is k-nearest neighbours imputation which is based on a variation of the Gower Distance for numerical, categorical, ordered and semi-continuous variables. To compute the Gower distance between two items you compare each element and compute a term. If the element is numeric, the term is the absolute value of the difference divided by the range. If the element is non-numeric the term is 1 if the elements are different or the term is 0 if the elements are the same. The Gower distance is the average of the terms. Each individual term will be between 0.0 and 1.0 inclusive, therefore the Gower distance will always be between 0.0 and 1.0 where a distance of 0.0 means the two items are the same and a distance of 1.0 means the two items are as far apart as possible, relative to the source data set.

```{r}
# Using KNN function in VIM package 
# k is the number of nearest neighbour donors used (k = 1 is Nearest Neighbour imputation)
# dist_var takes the variables to be used for distance calculation
# Here, variables have been chosen randomly but in a real method you would choose variables based upon relationships within your dataset

knn_imputation <- VIM::kNN(data = clean_survey_data, variable = "general_health", k = 4 ,  
                          dist_var = c("sex","employment_status", "days_unable_28d"))

# Display results

head(x = knn_imputation)
```

The imputed value for general_health is chosen randomly using 4 closest donors.
This is a very simple example of imputing using K Nearest Neighbours. Below, more detail is given on how custom functions may be created in order to conduct this and other imputation methods. 

### Excercise 

Impute the missing value in the hours_worked_away_7d variable for the fifth person using K-Nearest Neighbours. Because all of the missing hours_worked_away_7d values in the dataset are among employed people, restrict the donor pool first to employed respondents only. Tehn use the 5 closest donors for kNN, and use days_unable_28d, sex and employment_status as distance variables.

```{r}

# Select employed respondents only
employed_data <- clean_survey_data |>
  dplyr::filter(employment_status == "Employed")

# Using KNN function in VIM package 
# k is the number of nearest neighbour donors used

knn_imputation_cont <- VIM::kNN(data = employed_data, variable = "hours_worked_away_7d", k = 5,
                                dist_var = c("days_unable_28d", "sex", "employment_status"))


# Display results

knn_imputation_cont %>% 
   dplyr::select("hours_worked_away_7d", everything()) %>%  
   head()

```
The imputed value in the hours_worked_away_7d column is chosen randomly using 5 closest donors.


# Further exploration: How imputation methods can be implemented in code

The code examples so far have used established software packages to carry out commonly used imputation methods. Often when implementing imputation methods, statistical offices tailor and develop their own functions to meet the specific requirements of their data. The benefits of writing custom functions are that they can provide greater control over which values are imputed and how, allow specific rules and assumptions to be incorporated, and make the individual steps in the imputation process more transparent.

The following examples demonstrate how some of the methods introduced above could be implemented using custom functions. These examples are intended to help you understand what is happening behind the scenes when an imputation method is applied. In a real world scenario, these functions can be tailored more specifically based upon the dataset and specific imputation requirements.

## Mean imputation

```{r}

#' Mean Imputation
#'
#' Performs mean imputation on one or more numeric variables.
#' An imputation flag is also created to identify imputed values.
#'
#' @param df A data frame containing the variables to be imputed.
#' @param variables A character vector containing the names of the
#'   variables to impute.
#'
#' @return A data frame containing the imputed values and an imputation
#'   flag. 
#'
#' @examples
#' mean_data <- mean_impute(
#'   df = clean_survey_data,
#'   variables = c("age", "days_unable_28d")
#' )
#'

mean_impute <- function(df, variables) {
  
  for (variable in variables) {
    
    # Convert to numeric
    df[[variable]] <- as.numeric(df[[variable]])
    
    # Create an imputation flag
    df[[paste0(variable, "_imputed")]] <- is.na(df[[variable]])
    
    # Calculate the mean of observed values
    mean_value <- mean(df[[variable]], na.rm = TRUE)
    
    # Replace missing values with the mean
    df[[variable]][is.na(df[[variable]])] <- mean_value
  }
  
  return(df)
  
}

```

Now this function can be used to find the mean for variables in the dataset.

```{r}

# Use the function to find the mean for age and days_unable_28d

mean_data_custom <- mean_impute(clean_survey_data, c("age", "hours_worked_away_7d"))

```


## Regression imputation

```{r}

#' Regression Imputation
#'
#' Imputes missing values using deterministic or stochastic linear regression
#' and creates an imputation flag.
#'
#' @param df A data frame containing the variables.
#' @param variable_to_impute Name of the numeric variable to impute.
#' @param predictor_variables Character vector of predictor variable names.
#' @param stochastic If TRUE, adds a randomly sampled residual to each prediction.
#'
#' @return A data frame containing the imputed values and imputation flag.
#'
#' @examples
#' reg_data <- reg_impute(
#'   df = employed_data,
#'   variable_to_impute = "hours_worked_away_7d",
#'   predictor_variables = c("age", "sex"),
#'   stochastic = FALSE
#' )
#'
reg_impute <- function(
  df,
  variable_to_impute,
  predictor_variables,
  stochastic = FALSE
) {
  
  # Create imputation flag
  flag_name <- paste0(variable_to_impute, "_imputed")
  df[[flag_name]] <- is.na(df[[variable_to_impute]])
  
  # Create regression formula
  formula <- as.formula(
    paste(
      variable_to_impute,
      "~",
      paste(predictor_variables, collapse = " + ")
    )
  )
  
  # Fit linear regression model using observed values
  model <- lm(
    formula,
    data = df
  )
  
  # Identify rows that need imputing
  missing_rows <- is.na(df[[variable_to_impute]])
  
  # Predict values for the missing cases
  predicted_values <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = df[missing_rows, ]
  )
  
  # If stochastic imputation is selected
  if (stochastic) {
    
    # Get residuals from the regression model
    residuals <- residuals(model)
    
    # Add a randomly selected residual to each prediction
    predicted_values <- predicted_values +
      sample(
        residuals,
        size = length(predicted_values),
        replace = TRUE
      )
  }
    
  # Prevent negative imputed values
  predicted_values[predicted_values < 0] <- 0
  
  # Replace missing values with predicted values
  df[[variable_to_impute]][missing_rows] <- predicted_values
  
  # Return completed dataset
  return(df)
}
```


Now this function can be used to impute for missing variables in the dataset. Below, `hours_worked_away_7d` will be imputed using `age` and `sex` as predictor variables.
```{r}


# Run deterministic imputation on employed_data
deter_reg_data_custom <- reg_impute(
  df = employed_data,
  variable_to_impute = "hours_worked_away_7d",
  predictor_variables = c(
    "age",
    "sex"
  )
)

# Run stochastic imputation on employed_data
sto_reg_data_custom <- reg_impute(
  df = employed_data,
  variable_to_impute = "hours_worked_away_7d",
  predictor_variables = c(
    "age",
    "sex"
  ),
  stochastic = TRUE
)

```




## KNN imputation

```{r}

#' K-Nearest Neighbour Imputation
#'
#' Imputes missing values using K-nearest neighbour (KNN) imputation
#' and creates an imputation flag.
#'
#' @param df A data frame containing the variables.
#' @param variables_to_impute Character vector of variable names to impute.
#' @param distance_variables Character vector of variables used to find similar records.
#' @param k Number of nearest neighbours to use. Default is 5.
#'
#' @return A data frame containing the imputed values and imputation flags.
#'
#' @examples
#' knn_data <- knn_impute(
#'   df = employed_data,
#'   variables_to_impute = "hours_worked_away_7d",
#'   distance_variables = c("age", "sex"),
#'   k = 5
#' )
#'

knn_impute <- function(
  df,
  variables_to_impute,
  distance_variables,
  k = 5
) {
  
  
  # Check that all specified variables exist
  required_variables <- unique(
    c(variables_to_impute, distance_variables)
  )
  
  missing_variables <- setdiff(required_variables, names(df))
  
  if (length(missing_variables) > 0) {
    stop(
      "These variables were not found in the data: ",
      paste(missing_variables, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }
  
  # Loop through variables being imputed
  for (variable in variables_to_impute) {
    
    # Create imputation flag: TRUE = imputed, FALSE = observed
    df[[paste0(variable, "_imputed")]] <- 
      is.na(df[[variable]])
  }

  # Select variables needed for KNN
  knn_variables <- unique(
    c(variables_to_impute, distance_variables)
  )
  
  knn_data <- df[knn_variables]
  
  # Carry out KNN imputation
  imputed_values <- VIM::kNN(
    knn_data,
    variable = variables_to_impute,
    dist_var = distance_variables,
    k = k,
    imp_var = FALSE
  )
  
  # Copy the imputed variables back into the full dataset
  df[variables_to_impute] <- 
    imputed_values[variables_to_impute]
  
  # Return the completed dataset
  return(df)
}

```


Now using this function, impute hours_worked_away_7d using age and sex. As hours_worked_away_7d is only missing for employed individuals, the code subsets by this first. 

```{r}

knn_data_custom <- clean_survey_data

# Keep only employed people
employed_data <- clean_survey_data[clean_survey_data$employment_status == "Employed", ]
  
# Run knn imputatiom

knn_employed_impute <- knn_impute(
  df = employed_data,
  variables_to_impute = c(
    "hours_worked_away_7d"
  ),
  distance_variables = c(
    "employment_status",
    "age",
    "sex"
  ),
  k = 5
)

# Create the imputation flag in the main dataset
knn_data_custom$hours_worked_away_7d_imputed <- FALSE

# Identify employed rows
employed_rows <- knn_data_custom$employment_status == "Employed"

# Copy the imputed values back into the main dataset
knn_data_custom$hours_worked_away_7d[employed_rows] <-
```
